chunks: Explain PFM operation in a buck. The question: Explain PFM operation.
PFM stands for pulse-frequency modulation. It is a light-load mode in which the converter does not switch at a fixed rate.
Instead, it sends a small fixed-size pulse of energy to the output only when the output has sagged, then sleeps. The lighter the load, the less often it fires.
Imagine a leaky bucket that must stay near full. You have a small ladle. Whenever the level drops a little, you add one ladle-full. If the leak is slow, you add one rarely.
If the leak is fast, you add one often. Every ladle is the same size.
The analogy breaks down in that the "ladle" is a triangle of inductor current that must start and end at zero.
In single-pulse PFM the converter returns to sleep after each pulse; in burst mode it can chain several pulses until the output reaches an upper threshold, then sleep for longer.
Pulse: one burst of inductor current that ramps up, then ramps down to zero. Peak current: the fixed height each pulse ramps up to.
Threshold: the output voltage at which the controller fires the next pulse. Sleep: the idle time between pulses, with both switches off and the capacitor feeding the load.
PWM: the fixed-frequency mode PFM replaces at light load ("Buck operating modes (CCM, DCM, PFM)").
Say each pulse delivers 0. 5 µC of charge to the output. A 10 milliamps load takes 0. 01 coulombs (C, the unit of charge) every second, so it needs 0. 01 over 0.
5 micro equals 20 000 pulses per second. At 1 milliamps the load needs only 2,000 pulses per second. The pulses look the same in both cases, but come less often at light load.
"PFM is a light-load mode where the converter fires fixed-size pulses only when the output droops below a threshold.
Each pulse ramps the inductor to a fixed peak, then it discharges to zero into the output, and the converter sleeps until the output sags again.
Pulse rate is proportional to load, so switching losses scale down with the load and efficiency stays high.
The trade-offs are more, lower-frequency ripple and a slower response to a sudden load step."
